findings.description: ため息が堪えられない describes being unable to suppress a sigh of admiration. A forced deep breath substitutes a different response.

contexts.japanese: 幼い私が見ても、その美しさにため息が堪えられないほどに。
contexts.japanesePC: 幼い私が見ても、その美しさにため息が堪えられないほどに。
contexts.japanesePS3: 幼い私が見ても、その美しさにため息が堪えられないほどに。
contexts.WH: Even as young as I was, it still forced me to take a deep breath when I witnessed its beauty.
contexts.MG: Even as young as I was, it still forced me to take a deep breath when I witnessed its beauty.
contexts.UP: Even as young as I was, it still forced me to take a deep breath when I witnessed its beauty.
contexts.note: Both editions retain “forced me to take a deep breath,” substituting breathing for an irrepressible sigh of admiration.

findings.sourceReading: Even the young narrator cannot help sighing at the vase’s beauty.
findings.alternative: Both suggest being affected by beauty, but a deep inhalation does not express the involuntary admiring sigh.

findings.description: もっともお気に入りのコレクションのひとつ identifies one of Grandfather’s most treasured collectibles. The English attaches favorite to the collection as a whole instead.

contexts.japanese: もちろんそれは、お祖父さまにとってもっともお気に入りのコレクションのひとつ。
contexts.japanesePC: もちろんそれは、お祖父さまにとってもっともお気に入りのコレクションのひとつ。
contexts.japanesePS3: もちろんそれは、お祖父さまにとってもっともお気に入りのコレクションのひとつ。
contexts.WH: Of course, that was a member of Grandfather's favorite collection.
contexts.MG: Of course, it was a member of Grandfather's favorite collection.
contexts.UP: Of course, it was one of Grandfather's favorite collection pieces.
contexts.note: MG retains “member of Grandfather’s favorite collection.” UP restores one of his favorite collection pieces.

findings.sourceReading: The vase is among Grandfather’s most treasured collection pieces.
findings.alternative: English collection can loosely include the favorite items; the item-specific emphasis is nevertheless weakened.

findings.description: 軽やかに見えながら物言わぬ重厚感 contrasts apparent lightness with silent gravitas. Just glancing at it gave it an indescribable sense of dignity drops that contrast and makes the glance confer dignity.

contexts.japanese: このような透き通るようで、だけれども気品があって、軽やかに見えながら物言わぬ重厚感があり。
contexts.japanesePC: このような透き通るようで、だけれども気品があって、軽やかに見えながら物言わぬ重厚感があり。
contexts.japanesePS3: このような透き通るようで、だけれども気品があって、軽やかに見えながら物言わぬ重厚感があり。
contexts.WH: It was transparent and yet so elegant that just glancing at it gave it an indescribable sense of dignity.
contexts.MG: It looked light...and yet so elegant that just glancing at it gave it an indescribable sense of dignity.
contexts.UP: You could almost see right through it, and yet it was so elegant; it appeared so weightless, and yet it had an indescribable presence.
contexts.note: MG retains the lost transparency/lightness contrast and makes the glance confer dignity. UP restores the visual contrasts and weighty presence.

findings.sourceReading: The vase seems translucent yet refined, light yet silently imposing.
findings.alternative: Dignity captures part of 重厚感, but not its tension with lightness or its silent quality.

findings.description: 触れてはならぬものだからこそ explains this degree of beauty by its being something one must not touch. Because something this beautiful should not be touched reverses the explanatory relation.

contexts.japanese: これほどの美しさは、触れてはならぬものだからこそ。
contexts.japanesePC: これほどの美しさは、触れてはならぬものだからこそ。
contexts.japanesePS3: これほどの美しさは、触れてはならぬものだからこそ。
contexts.WH: Because something this beautiful shouldn't be touched.
contexts.MG: Something this beautiful should never be touched.
contexts.UP: This much beauty arises precisely because it must never be touched.
contexts.note: MG retains the reversed relation, saying the vase must not be touched because it is beautiful. UP says its beauty arises precisely because it must not be touched.

findings.sourceReading: It has such beauty precisely because it is something forbidden to the touch, a beauty dwelling only in extreme fragility.
findings.alternative: The next line retains fragility and supports the same prohibition, but the immediate causal relation is reversed.

contexts.japanesePC: 黄金の燐粉で幻想的に輝きながら、その美しき蝶が一匹、二匹と集まります。
contexts.japanesePS3: 黄金の燐粉で幻想的に輝きながら、その美しき蝶が一匹、二匹と集まります。
contexts.WH: As mysteriously glowing golden dots shone, the beautiful butterflies began to gather, one at a time.
contexts.MG: As mysteriously glowing golden dots shone in the air, the butterflies began to gather, one at a time.
contexts.UP: The beautiful butterflies began to gather, one at a time, glittering fantastically with glowing golden powder.
contexts.note: MG retains detached glowing dots. UP restores the butterflies glittering with golden powder.

findings.sourceReading: The beautiful butterflies gather, shining fantastically with golden scale dust.
findings.alternative: Dots could evoke tiny particles, but their relation to the butterfly surface is lost.

findings.description: Became a group. and there, became the witch’s form separates a lowercase conjunction with a period and leaves the transformation clause without a workable subject.

contexts.japanese: 蝶が次々と集まって群れとなると、そこには彼女の姿が…。
contexts.japanesePC: 蝶が次々と集まって群となると、そこには彼女の姿が…。
contexts.japanesePS3: 蝶が次々と集まって群れとなると、そこには彼女の姿が…。
contexts.WH: The butterflies gathered one after another and became a group. and there, became the witch's form...
contexts.MG: The butterflies kept gathering until they formed a cloud, ...and then she was there...
contexts.UP: The butterflies gathered one after another, grouped together, and there, became her form...
contexts.note: MG replaces the broken clause with a cloud forming and Beatrice appearing. UP makes the gathered butterflies the subject of becoming her form; its punctuation remains awkward, but the original sentence-fragment failure is repaired.

findings.sourceReading: As butterflies gather into a swarm, her figure appears there.
findings.alternative: The transformation is recoverable, but the English sentence is malformed.

findings.description: 一度言い聞かせたこと refers to something he has already instructed the child about. Failed to follow something he said even once relocates once onto the disobedience.

contexts.japanese: そして、一度言い聞かせたことが守られなかった時は、地獄の堕天使も震え上がるほどに怒りくるうのです。
contexts.japanesePC: そして、一度言い聞かせたことが守られなかった時は、地獄の堕天使も震え上がるほどに怒り狂うのです。
contexts.japanesePS3: そして、一度言い聞かせたことが守られなかった時は、地獄の堕天使も震え上がるほどに怒りくるうのです。
contexts.WH: And when you failed to follow something he said even once, he would become so mad, with a rage that would make even the fallen angels in hell quiver.
contexts.MG: And when you failed to follow something he said even once, he would become so mad, with a rage that would make even the fallen angels in hell quiver.
contexts.UP: And once he told you something, if you failed to follow it, he would become mad with a rage that would make even the fallen angels in hell quiver.
contexts.note: MG retains “failed ... even once,” attaching once to disobedience. UP restores the condition as failing an instruction already given.

findings.sourceReading: Kinzo rages when an instruction he has already given is not followed.
findings.alternative: Both describe intolerant anger; the threshold shifts from prior instruction to even a single failure.

findings.description: 折檻 denotes punitive chastisement, stronger than being scolded. The earlier English punishment at 83107 shows that the threatened consequence was not consistently limited to verbal reprimand.

contexts.japanese:
「零してしまった姫様の涙を掬う魔法は持ち合わせておりませんが、
姫様がお館様から折檻を受けなくて済むようにする魔法なら、何とかなるかもしれません」
contexts.japanesePC: 「零してしまった姫様の涙を掬う魔法は持ち合わせておりませんが、姫様がお館様から折檻を受けなくて済むようにする魔法なら、何とかなるかもしれません。」
contexts.japanesePS3:
「零してしまった姫様の涙を掬う魔法は持ち合わせておりませんが、
姫様がお館様から折檻を受けなくて済むようにする魔法なら、何とかなるかもしれません」
contexts.WH: "I hold no magic to scoop up your fallen tears, princess, but if you want magic that will make it possible for you to avoid being scolded by the Master, I might be able to do something."
contexts.MG:
"I possess no magic that can scoop up your fallen tears, princess,
but if you need magic that will prevent the Master from scolding you, I might be able to manage something."
contexts.UP:
"I hold no magic to scoop up your fallen tears, princess,
but if you want magic that will make it possible for you to avoid being scolded by the Master, I might be able to do something."
contexts.note: Both editions reduce 折檻 to being scolded, despite translating the same threatened consequence as punishment at row 41.

findings.sourceReading: Beatrice may provide magic that spares the princess Kinzo’s punishment.
findings.alternative: The scene also uses 叱る and later お叱り, so scolding is part of the threat; it nevertheless softens this specifically stronger term.

findings.description: 無限の魔力が備わる says endless magical power is acquired at that level. Considered to be an Endless Witch substitutes a title or classification for the attainment, and supplies the title before the next Japanese reveal.

contexts.japanese:
その境地に達した時、無限の魔力が備わるでしょう。
それこそが、魔女の達するべき無限の境地。
私たちはその魔女を、最大の敬いをもってこう呼びます」
「無限の魔女…」
contexts.japanesePC: 「えぇ。その境地に達した時、無限の魔力が備わるでしょう。それこそが、魔女の達するべき無限の境地。私たちはその魔女を、最大の敬いをもってこう呼びます。」
contexts.japanesePS3:
その境地に達した時、無限の魔力が備わるでしょう。
それこそが、魔女の達するべき無限の境地。
私たちはその魔女を、最大の敬いをもってこう呼びます」
「無限の魔女…」
contexts.WH: "Yes.  When one reaches that level they are considered to be an Endless Witch.  That is the endless level that all witches should reach.  We respect those witches the most and call them this."
contexts.MG:
When one reaches that level, they are considered to be an Endless Witch.
That is the endless level that all witches ought to reach.
We offer the utmost respect to those witches and call them by that title."
"An Endless Witch..."
contexts.UP:
When one reaches that level, they are possessed of endless magical power.
That is the endless level that all witches should strive to reach.
As a sign of the highest respect to those witches, we call them..."
"An Endless Witch..."
contexts.note: MG prematurely substitutes the Endless Witch title for acquiring endless magical power. UP restores the power attainment and leaves the title reveal to the following lines.

findings.sourceReading: Upon reaching the level of repeated restoration, a witch possesses endless magic; the honorific name is then introduced.
findings.alternative: Later explanation preserves endless restoration and the title, so this is a local mechanism-to-classification change and timing shift, not an unsolvability finding.

findings.description: 有難味を感じる means appreciating the worth of what she has attained. Feel valued changes her gratitude or appreciation into receiving validation.

contexts.japanese:
「…たまには有難味を感じねば、少々勿体無いというものよ。
……くっくくくくく」
contexts.japanesePC: …たまには有難味を感じねば、少々勿体無いというものよ。……くっくくくくく。」
contexts.japanesePS3:
「…たまには有難味を感じねば、少々勿体無いというものよ。
……くっくくくくく」

contexts.MG:

...*cackle*cackle*cackle*."

......*cackle*cackle*cackle*."

findings.sourceReading: Beatrice thinks she ought occasionally to appreciate the title earned through long training.
findings.alternative: Feeling satisfied by the title is preserved in the preceding line, but feeling valued adds an interpersonal validation sense absent here.

findings.description: 自分の言葉 refers to Beatrice’s own preceding words: the remembered teaching seems to answer them. As though answering herself assigns the reflexive to Teacher.

contexts.japanese:
“修行に終わりはありませんよ。
永遠の境地に辿り着いた、と思った時こそが、その未熟さを悔いる時なのです。”
……自分の言葉に答えるかのように、そんなことを言っていたのを思い出す。
contexts.japanesePC: ……自分の言葉に答えるかのように、そんなことを言っていたのを思い出す。
contexts.japanesePS3:
“修行に終わりはありませんよ。
永遠の境地に辿り着いた、と思った時こそが、その未熟さを悔いる時なのです。”
……自分の言葉に答えるかのように、そんなことを言っていたのを思い出す。
contexts.WH: ......I remember her saying something like that as though answering herself.
contexts.MG:
'Training has no end.
When you think you've reached the eternal level, that's exactly the time to bemoan your own immaturity.'
...I recalled those words as though she'd answered me directly.
contexts.UP:
― Training has no end.
When you think you have reached the eternal level, that is the time to regret your immaturity.
......As if in answer to my own words, a memory of her saying something like that entered my mind.
contexts.note: MG makes Teacher’s remembered words answer Beatrice directly; UP explicitly makes them an answer to Beatrice’s own words. Both restore the reflexive referent.

findings.sourceReading: Beatrice recalls Teacher’s words as if they were a reply to her present question about happiness and the end of training.
findings.alternative: First-person I remember remains, but herself instead of me/my words makes Teacher answer her own remarks.

当の本人に思い出させるのが一番か。

今に泣きながら認めたくなるわ。
今だって、本当は哀れに土下座しながら許しを乞いたいくせにぃ！」
contexts.WH: "It's alright, we don't have to force him to accept it.  Right now he wants to accept it, crying.
contexts.MG:
"It's okay, we don't have to force him to accept it.
Soon, he'll wanna accept it so hard he'll start crying.

findings.sourceReading: They need not force acceptance: before long he will want to admit it in tears; she then claims even now he wants to beg forgiveness.
findings.alternative: The next statement already alleges present hidden surrender, mitigating the broader characterization change; the initial forecast still becomes present assertion.

findings.description: しくしくと、仕舞いにはわんわんと泣き出す describes the child first weeping quietly and eventually breaking into loud, unrestrained wailing. Breaking into tears and sobbing flattens that progression and loses the final intensity.

contexts.japanese: それに怯え、私はしくしくと、仕舞いにはわんわんと泣き出すのでした…。
contexts.japanesePC: それに怯え、私はしくしくと、仕舞いにはわんわんと泣き出すのでした…。
contexts.japanesePS3: それに怯え、私はしくしくと、仕舞いにはわんわんと泣き出すのでした…。
contexts.WH: Frightened, I ended up breaking into tears and sobbing...
contexts.MG: I ended up breaking into tears and sobbing, frightened...
contexts.UP: Frightened, I ended up breaking into tears and sobbing...
contexts.note: Both editions use the shared “breaking into tears and sobbing,” flattening the explicit escalation from quiet weeping to loud wailing.

findings.sourceReading: Terrified of Grandfather’s punishment, the child’s crying escalates from quiet weeping until she is bawling loudly.
findings.alternative: Tears and sobbing communicates sustained distress, and English sobbing can be loud, but it does not preserve the explicit quiet-to-loud progression or the eventual wail.

findings.description: The surrounding narration is Beatrice’s first-person interior monologue, marked explicitly by 妾 before and after this sentence. She shook her head lightly abruptly changes the unexpressed Japanese subject into an external third-person narrator.

contexts.japanese: 緩やかに頭を振る。
contexts.japanesePC: 緩やかに頭を振る。
contexts.japanesePS3: 緩やかに頭を振る。
contexts.WH: She shook her head lightly.
contexts.MG: She shook her head lightly.
contexts.UP: I shook my head lightly.
contexts.note: MG retains an external “She” inside Beatrice’s first-person monologue. UP restores “I shook my head.”

findings.sourceReading: While reflecting on the Endless Witch title in her own voice, Beatrice lightly shakes her head and continues her monologue.
findings.alternative: English prose can briefly use external narration inside a focalized passage, and the referent of she is clear.

findings.description: 卿の称号を持つ大魔女とて恐れるほど says boredom is so dangerous that even Great Witches bearing the title Lady fear it. This is frighteningly true instead makes the preceding proposition itself frightening and loses those witches as the experiencers of fear.

退屈は全ての魔女を殺す最悪の毒。
……卿の称号を持つ大魔女とて恐れるほどの。
永遠の至福に辿り着いた故に苛む、永遠の毒…。
contexts.japanesePC: ……卿の称号を持つ大魔女とて恐れるほどの。
contexts.japanesePS3:
退屈は全ての魔女を殺す最悪の毒。
……卿の称号を持つ大魔女とて恐れるほどの。

contexts.WH: ......To the Great Witches who are given the title 'Lady', this is frighteningly true.
contexts.MG:
Boredom is the worst sort of poison, which kills all witches.
...Even those Great Witches who are given the title "Lady" fear it.
It's the eternal poison that tortures them because of the eternal bliss they've reached...
contexts.UP:
Boredom is the worst poison that kills all witches.
......To the Great Witches who hold the title "Lady", this is frighteningly true.
It is the eternal poison that tortures them because of the eternal bliss that they have reached...
contexts.note: MG explicitly says even titled Great Witches fear boredom. UP retains the original-WH shift by saying the proposition is “frighteningly true.”

findings.sourceReading: Beatrice calls boredom the worst poison to witches, feared even by the highest titled Great Witches.
findings.alternative: Calling the statement frighteningly true preserves the idea that boredom is gravely dangerous to powerful witches.

findings.description: 静かにせぬか、やかましい is an angry demand that the sisters be quiet because they are noisy. Couldn’t you be silent, shut up combines a question and command with broken punctuation and contradictory conversational force.

contexts.japanese: 「静かにせぬか、やかましいッ！！」
contexts.japanesePC: 「静かにせぬか、やかましいッ！！」
contexts.japanesePS3: 「静かにせぬか、やかましいッ！！」

contexts.UP: "Can you not be silent, shut up!!"
contexts.note: MG replaces the broken construction with a natural complaint about the infernal racket. UP changes “Couldn’t” to “Can you not” but still splices “be silent, shut up” into one malformed command.

findings.sourceReading: Beatrice bellows at the noisy Stakes to be quiet, frightening all seven into hiding.
findings.alternative: Both English fragments demand silence, so the intended outburst remains obvious despite the malformed combination.

findings.description: 告げる here means Beatrice speaks or proclaims before chanting. And I told is incomplete English because tell requires an object or recipient in this use.

そして告げる。
詠う。
思い出させる。

妾は黄金の煙管を振り上げる。

詠う。
思い出させる。

I chanted.

findings.description: 誰が誰と connects the scattered pieces as who belonged with whom, continuing their grotesque personification as they remember themselves. Which part should go with which part flattens them into ordinary parts, while where should join with where is also missing a grammatical subject.

誰が誰と繋がっていたのか。
どことどこがどう組みあがっていたのか。

findings.description: 駄目だな and 全然駄目だぜ repeat Battler’s characteristic evaluation that the alleged hell is no good or fails to measure up. That’s just useless and it’s all useless instead judge utility and lose the recurring verbal motif.

この程度で地獄かよ、駄目だな。
あぁ、全然駄目だぜ」
contexts.japanesePC: 「へ、…へへへへ。この程度で地獄かよ、駄目だな。あぁ、全然駄目だぜ。」
contexts.japanesePS3:
「へ、…へへへへ。
この程度で地獄かよ、駄目だな。
あぁ、全然駄目だぜ」

contexts.MG:
"Heh, ...hehehehe.
You call this hell? That's just useless.
Aah, it's all useless."

Yeah, that's no goddamn good at all."
contexts.note: MG retains “useless” twice. UP restores Battler’s recurring “no good” formulation, including its emphatic second use.

findings.sourceReading: Battler defiantly dismisses Beatrice’s torture as nowhere near good enough to count as hell, repeating his familiar “no good” phrasing.
findings.alternative: Useless remains a blunt negative judgment and can imply Beatrice’s attempt is ineffective against him.

findings.description: 虚勢など張らずに素直になれば tells Battler to stop bluffing or putting on a brave front and be honest with himself. Stayed obedient changes candor about his suffering into compliance or submission to the torturers.

contexts.japanese: 「虚勢など張らずに素直になれば、もっと楽になれるのに」
contexts.japanesePC: 「虚勢など張らずに素直になれば、もっと楽になれるのに。」
contexts.japanesePS3: 「虚勢など張らずに素直になれば、もっと楽になれるのに」
contexts.MG: "If you just stayed obedient instead of acting tough, this would go much easier."
contexts.UP: "If you stopped acting all tough and started being honest with yourself, this would be much easier on you."
contexts.note: MG retains “stayed obedient,” turning honesty into compliance. UP restores the contrast between acting tough and being honest with himself.

findings.sourceReading: A Stake says Battler would suffer less if he stopped acting tough and admitted his true feelings.
findings.alternative: 素直 can mean obedient, and the torturers do want Battler to submit, but 虚勢 establishes honesty about his bravado as the immediate contrast.

findings.description: どこを貫いちゃおう uses 貫く for piercing or stabbing through Battler and leads into the Stakes choosing body parts. Where should I strike weakens the specified penetrative violence to a generic blow.

findings.alternative: Strike can broadly describe an attack by a stake and the following body-part choices retain the violent context.

この身の程知らずが！」

contexts.japanesePS3:

contexts.MG:

Are you a moron?!

findings.description: 無限の蘇生は、無限の死をも自在にする states that endless resurrection also makes endless death freely controllable. Giving eternal rebirth and eternal death at will is a sentence fragment and loses the causal relation from resurrection to repeated death.

contexts.japanese: 無限の蘇生は、無限の死をも自在にする。
contexts.japanesePC: 無限の蘇生は、無限の死をも自在にする。
contexts.japanesePS3: 無限の蘇生は、無限の死をも自在にする。
contexts.WH: Giving eternal rebirth and eternal death at will.
contexts.MG: Giving eternal rebirth and eternal death at will.
contexts.UP: Endless rebirths give me free reign over endless deaths, too.
contexts.note: MG retains the fragment and lost causal relation. UP restores endless rebirths as what grants control over endless deaths.

findings.sourceReading: Because Beatrice can resurrect Battler endlessly, she can also subject him to death endlessly at will.
findings.alternative: The gerund phrase places eternal rebirth and death together under voluntary control, so the paired concepts remain visible.

findings.description: All death and life has no meaning gives the coordinated subject death and life a singular verb. Standard English requires have, and the reversed fixed pairing further roughens Beatrice’s declarative narration.

contexts.MG:

findings.sourceReading: Before Beatrice as the Endless Witch, every life and death is meaningless because neither state permits escape.
findings.alternative: Life and death can be conceptualized collectively as one cycle, making the intended assertion entirely clear.

findings.description: UP uses the past perfect “the vase had been broken” at the exact moment the child broke it, making the vase sound already broken before her act rather than stating the resulting fact that “the vase was broken.”

contexts.japanese: …私が壷を割ってしまった時点で、“壷は割れた”のです。
contexts.japanesePS3: …私が壷を割ってしまった時点で、“壷は割れた”のです。

findings.sourceReading: The narrator says that from the moment she broke the vase, the fact or fate “the vase was broken” had been established.
findings.alternative: Past perfect can locate the broken state before the later retrospective explanation, but its placement after “at the time that I broke” strongly invites an earlier-than-breaking reading.
